sections.h: Simon and the charter of the dynasty
sections.b:
After Jonathan was captured and killed (about 143 BC), the people acclaimed Simon, the last of Mattathias's sons, as their leader (1 Maccabees 13:1–9). Under him Judea stopped paying tribute (142 BC), dated its contracts by his years, and took the Citadel of Jerusalem (141 BC). In September 140 BC an assembly of priests, people and elders made him "leader and high priest forever, until a faithful prophet arises" (1 Maccabees 14:41), with command of the army and the sole right to wear purple. This decree, set up on bronze tablets on Mount Zion, is the charter of the Hasmonean house: the office passes to Simon's sons.

The family was priestly, of the course of Jehoiarib (1 Chronicles 24:7), but not of the line of Zadok, and the clause about a prophet may answer those who doubted their right. Simon was murdered by his son-in-law at Dok in 134 BC, and his son John Hyrcanus succeeded him (1 Maccabees 16:11–24).

sections.h: A history written for the dynasty
sections.b: 1 Maccabees ends by pointing to the annals of John Hyrcanus's high priesthood (1 Maccabees 16:23–24), so it was probably written around 100 BC, late in his reign or soon after his death in 104 BC. It tells the family's story as the story of Israel's deliverance: the poem of 1 Maccabees 14:4–15 describes Simon's rule in the words of Micah 4:4 and Zechariah 8:4. Later verdicts were less kind. The Pharisees asked John Hyrcanus to give up the high priesthood (Josephus, Antiquities 13.288–292), the Talmud tells a similar story of a Hasmonean king (Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 66a), and the Psalms of Solomon, written after Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, accuse the family of seizing David's throne.

From 152 BC rival claimants fought over the Seleucid throne, and each bid for Jewish support. 1 Maccabees 12–15 shows the last stage. Tryphon, a general who first ruled in the name of the boy king Antiochus VI, captured and killed Jonathan and then murdered the boy and took the crown (1 Maccabees 12:39–13:32). His rival Demetrius II freed Judea from tribute in 142 BC (1 Maccabees 13:36–41), and was later captured by the Parthians (1 Maccabees 14:1–3). Demetrius's brother Antiochus VII promised Simon everything, including the right to mint coins, and then demanded back Joppa, Gazara and the Citadel once he had defeated Tryphon (1 Maccabees 15:1–31). He went on to besiege Jerusalem under John Hyrcanus; only after his death in Parthia in 129 BC did the kingdom stop threatening Judea.

Long before Revelation's beast, Rome appears in Jewish writing as a protector. Jonathan renewed Judas's treaty with the Senate (1 Maccabees 12:1–4), the Senate renewed it with Simon, who sent a great gold shield (1 Maccabees 14:16–24), and a consul wrote to the kings and cities of the east forbidding them to harm the Jews (1 Maccabees 15:15–24). The friendship gave diplomatic cover but no soldiers. It ended in 63 BC when Pompey, called in by quarreling Hasmonean brothers, took Jerusalem; the Psalms of Solomon mourn the result.

1 Maccabees says three times that no prophet was speaking in its day: the defiled altar stones were stored until a prophet should come (1 Maccabees 4:46), the distress after Judas's death was the worst since prophets ceased (1 Maccabees 9:27), and Simon was made high priest "forever, until a faithful prophet arises" (1 Maccabees 14:41). Josephus (Against Apion 1.41) and the rabbis (Tosefta Sotah 13:3) also held that the line of prophets had ended with Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi. The hope that a prophet would come again is seen in John 1:21 and 6:14; Christians identify him with Christ, the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15; Acts 3:22).

sections.h: A golden age without a messiah: Simon
sections.b: The poem in praise of Simon (1 Maccabees 14:4–15) borrows the language of the prophets' age of blessing: each one under his vine and his fig tree (Micah 4:4), old men in the squares (Zechariah 8:4). Yet the book never calls Simon an anointed one or a son of David, and the decree for him looks for a prophet still to come (1 Maccabees 14:41). Jonathan Goldstein argued that the author meant readers to see the prophecies fulfilled in the Hasmoneans; others read the poem as praise in biblical style. A few decades later the Psalms of Solomon 17 looked for a son of David to replace the Hasmoneans.

Jonathan became high priest in 152 BC by a Seleucid king's appointment; Simon received the office "forever" by decree of the people in 140 BC (1 Maccabees 14:41). The family was of the priestly course of Jehoiarib (1 Chronicles 24:7), not of the house of Zadok, which had held the office since Solomon (1 Kings 2:35). The decree joined the high priesthood with the army and the government. Augustus's decree in Josephus calls Hyrcanus II "high priest of God Most High" (Antiquities 16.163), and the rabbis remembered contracts dated by "Yohanan, high priest of God Most High": the title of Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18), and some see Psalm 110:4 in the background. Hebrews later takes up the same psalm for Christ (Hebrews 7).

sections.h: Priest and ruler in one man
sections.b: The decree of 140 BC made Simon high priest, general and ethnarch together (1 Maccabees 14:41–47). In Israel's history the offices had usually been held by different men (Numbers 27:21; Zechariah 4:14), though Zechariah 6:11–13 and Melchizedek point the other way, and Chronicles tells how King Uzziah was struck with skin disease for burning incense (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Some Jews objected: the Pharisees asked John Hyrcanus to give up the high priesthood (Josephus, Antiquities 13.288–292), and a Talmudic story has a sage tell a Hasmonean king to leave the priestly crown to the seed of Aaron (Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 66a).

Simon decreed that the day the Citadel fell, the twenty-third of the second month (spring 141 BC), should be kept every year (1 Maccabees 13:50–52), as Judas had done for the Temple's dedication and the defeat of Nicanor. The Scroll of Fasts (Megillat Ta'anit) still lists the day among those on which Jews might not fast. Like Purim (Esther 9:20–28), these were feasts added after the Law, for later deliverances.

Simon brought Jonathan's bones home to Modein, as David brought Saul's and Jonathan's bones home (2 Samuel 21:12–14), and built a monument of seven pyramids for his parents and brothers, with columns carved with armor and ships, visible from the sea (1 Maccabees 13:25–30). It was in the style of Greek royal tombs. Josephus says it still stood in his day.

When Antiochus VII demanded back Joppa and Gazara, Simon answered, "We hold the inheritance of our ancestors, which our enemies wrongfully seized for a time" (1 Maccabees 15:33). He argues from the promise of the land, as Jephthah did with the king of Ammon (Judges 11:15–27), and Joshua 13:1–6 counts the coast among the land still to be taken. The Hasmoneans went on to conquer Idumea, Samaria and Galilee.

A letter in 1 Maccabees claims that the Spartans and the Jews are brothers, "from Abraham's family" (1 Maccabees 12:21). Greeks often found kinship between peoples in shared ancestors; Jewish writers linked the sons Abraham had by Keturah with far peoples (Genesis 25:1–4; Josephus, Antiquities 1.239–241). Erich Gruen, like Hengel and Bickerman before him, thinks the claim a Jewish construction; Jonathan Goldstein, Katzoff and others defend the letter. Either way it shows Abraham as father of many nations (Genesis 17:4–5) put to diplomatic use.

In 1 Maccabees "Mount Zion" means the Temple hill, distinct from the Citadel in the City of David, which the Seleucids held until 141 BC (1 Maccabees 13:49–52). Simon strengthened the Temple hill and lived there, and the decree in his honor was set up on bronze tablets on pillars on Mount Zion (1 Maccabees 14:26–27).

For a quarter century a Seleucid garrison held the Citadel beside the Temple. Jonathan began a wall to cut it off (1 Maccabees 12:36–37), and in spring 141 BC Simon starved it into surrender and entered it with palm branches and music (1 Maccabees 13:49–52). Excavations in the City of David have uncovered fortifications that some archaeologists identify with it.

The revolt ended not in one victory but in a slow winning of freedom. After Judas's death his brothers Jonathan and Simon used the Seleucid civil wars to win concessions. Tryphon killed Jonathan (about 143 BC); Simon won freedom from tribute in 142 BC, "the yoke of the Gentiles was lifted from Israel" (1 Maccabees 13:41), took the Citadel in 141 BC, and was confirmed as hereditary high priest and ruler in 140 BC (1 Maccabees 14:41). 1 Maccabees ends with Simon's murder in 134 BC and his son John's succession.

sections.h: Rome and Sparta under Jonathan and Simon
sections.b: Jonathan renewed the treaty with Rome and wrote to Sparta, while saying the Jews needed no allies, "since the holy books in our hands give us encouragement" (1 Maccabees 12:9). Rome and Sparta renewed the friendship with Simon (1 Maccabees 14:16–24), and a Roman consul wrote to the kings of the east on the Jews' behalf (1 Maccabees 15:15–24). The book praises these treaties, but its own story shows their limits: no Roman soldier came when Antiochus VII broke his word (1 Maccabees 15:27). The prophets had warned against trusting in foreign powers (Isaiah 31:1).
